title: Why You Must Remind Students Of Their Purpose https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/07/05/why-you-must-remind-students-of-their-purpose/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin warns that without regular reminders, students drift into treating school as an obligation done to them rather than an opportunity for them, which saps motivation, energy, and creativity. He describes the downstream effects: goofing off, disengagement, muted enthusiasm, and a growing sense of entitlement. His remedy is explicit and frequent: tell students directly, in age-appropriate language, why school matters and why what the teacher offers is valuable, modeling this with a sample morning message. He argues this daily reminder of purpose is what unlocks intrinsic motivation and personal responsibility, especially when delivered by a teacher students already like and respect. The article frames purpose-reminding as a necessary companion to rapport-building rather than a substitute for it.
points: Without regular reminders of purpose, students drift into seeing school as an obligation rather than an opportunity.
This drift saps energy, creativity, and motivation, and grows into a sense of entitlement.
The remedy is telling students explicitly and often why school and the day's learning matter, adjusted to grade level.
A sample opening message models how to deliver this purpose statement with passion and specificity.
This reminder of purpose only lands with full force when delivered by a teacher students already like and admire.
quotes: If not reminded, and reminded often, your students will naturally slip into believing that school is just something they’re supposed to do.
This attitude can cause students to take their education for granted, to see it as a grind, as something they’re forced to do rather than what it is.
Doing anything begrudgingly, anything with the specter of having to do it hanging over your head, can be a dangerous thing.
It is the ‘why’ of school, after all, that cracks ajar the gates of learning.
You tell them. You tell them every day why they’re there, why what they’re doing is important, and why what you have to offer them is a most precious gift.
Coming from someone your students like and admire, and delivered with passion, this simple message—which will vary in depth depending on grade level—can be powerful and deeply impressionable.
